text: Spectral elements: high-order finite elements and 2D Poisson The spectral element method (SEM) partitions a domain into elements and approximates the field with high-degree local polynomials. It connects finite-element assembly with high-order approximation of smooth functions. This chapter adopts a continuous Galerkin Legendre GLL variant and a small reproducible two-dimensional Poisson problem. SEM belongs to the high-order finite-element family; finite elements in general are not restricted to linear elements. Element-local polynomials also differ from a single global Fourier expansion. A small linear-system residual alone does not imply a small continuous-PDE error. On the last h refinement, p2 SEM gives L2 order about 3.04 and H1-seminorm order 2.01; P1 FEM gives 1.97 and 0.99. At 225 free unknowns, L2 errors are about 2.49e−4 for SEM and 5.38e−3 for P1. At p6 on 2 x 2 elements, L2 error is about 3.78e−7. These observations depend on smoothness, boundaries, element geometry, quadrature and solver choices. They establish neither universal p convergence near singularities nor a speed/accuracy ranking for all problems. Curved elements, mixed velocity/pressure spaces and fluid coupling are outside this execution. Related implementations: Nek5000 and nekRS Nek5000 is a high-order spectral-element flow solver. nekRS is the related CPU/GPU successor described by the official project. Follow those links for their documentation and source. The small Python Poisson code does not execute or validate either flow solver or its performance. Patera’s original paper supplies historical bibliographic context; the implemented Legendre GLL variant is separately specified.
